lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Tiago (Mock Rodízio) | Lesson 1 -- The Update Nobody Read

listenings.text: Tiago, it's Michael. Listen, I just got off a call with our warehouse and they tell me the second batch is not coming this week. That was news to me. I am not calling to complain, I am calling because I found out from the wrong person. If something moves, I need to hear it from you first, even when there is nothing I can do about it. Can you send me something short every Monday? Not a long report. Just where we are and what is stuck. Thanks.

leadin_media.prompt: Listen to the voicemail. What is Michael actually asking for?
choices: A discount, because the batch is late.
A short, regular update from Tiago, before he hears it elsewhere.
A longer written report every week.

paras: Sofia coordinates production at a metal parts factory in Joinville. Every Friday afternoon, for two years, she wrote a status report for her American client. It was thorough. It had numbers, dates, the name of every supplier, and it was usually four hundred words long. She was proud of it, and she never missed one.

In March the client called her, upset. A shipment had slipped by ten days and he had found out from his own warehouse, not from her. Sofia opened her sent folder and found the report from three weeks earlier. The delay was there. It was in the fourth paragraph, in the middle of a long sentence about tooling.
So the information had been sent, and the information had not arrived. Those are two different things, and she had been measuring the wrong one.

She changed the format that same week. Not four hundred words on Friday, but sixty seconds on Monday, on the phone, always in the same order: where we are, what is stuck, what I need from you, when it closes. If nothing was stuck, she said so, and the call took twenty seconds.
Nobody ever thanked her for the long reports. Four months into the short calls, the client asked her to explain the format to his other two suppliers.

gist.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: A client stopped reading reports because he was too busy.
Sending information is not the same as making it arrive.
Long reports are the safest way to protect yourself at work.

post_skill.title: Talk about it
items: Sofia's report was complete and still failed. Has that ever happened to something you wrote?
Sixty seconds on the phone, or four hundred words in writing — which one would your client prefer? And which one would you prefer?
She calls even when nothing is stuck. Is that a waste of time, or is it the point?
In your job, who finds things out too late — and why?

language_focus.title: Analyse and answer
items: Sofia says all five in under a minute. What order does she put them in, and why that order?
Two of the five are about the problem. Three are about what happens next. Which are which?
Line 2 says about four days, not four days. Why the about?
If you removed line 4, what would the client be left with?

language_focus.title: Reveal answer key
list: Order: where we are (1) → the gap (2) → the cause (3) → what I need from you (4) → when it closes (5). Status first, then the ask — never the other way around.
Problem: 2 and 3. What happens next: 1, 4 and 5.
About buys a small margin and still commits to a number. Four days exactly invites a fight about the fourth day; no number at all sounds like hiding.
News with no ask — the client hears a problem and has nothing to do with it. Line 4 is what turns an update into a conversation.
language_focus.note: Do not hand over this order as a rule before he finds it. Ask, wait, then open.

practice_a.text: Now take ONE of the four and say the whole update out loud: where you are, what is stuck, what you need, and when it closes. Then do it again with a real job of yours from this week.

practice_b.title: Reveal answer key
list: The blocker is the tooling — it arrived late.
We're on track for the date we agreed.
We're running about a week behind.
What I need from you is a decision on the packaging.
By Friday we'll have the documents ready for you.
practice_b.note: Accept justified variations: if it fits in one breath and says the same thing, it counts.

items: Case 1 — the good week
Nothing is stuck. Both batches left on time and the client has heard nothing from you since Monday. You still have to make the call.
Case 2 — the supplier
The tooling supplier moved the lead time from three weeks to five. Production slips by nine days. There is a second supplier, more expensive, who could do it in two.
Case 3 — your own mistake
The shipment is four days late because your team sent it to the old address. Nobody outside knows why yet. The client is going to ask.
Case 4 — waiting on him
You cannot start the second batch without the client's sign-off on the packaging. You asked twice. It has been eleven days.

production.title: Give the update
items: Take Case 1. Give the whole update out loud, without stopping. Sixty seconds, even though nothing is wrong.
Now Case 2. Where you are, what is stuck, what you need from him, when it closes — in that order.
Case 3 is the only one where the blocker is you. What is your first sentence — and what do you NOT say first?
In Case 4 the person who is late is the client. How do you say that without making it an accusation?
Which of the four would you rather send as a message than say on a call? Defend it.

production.label: Useful language
items: We're on track for ...
We're running about ... behind.
The blocker is ...
What I need from you is ...
By ... we'll have ...
Nothing is stuck on our side.
That one is on us.
I wanted you to hear it from me first.
It moves the date by about ...
Once we have that, we can start the same day.

discussion.title: Discussion
items: Is a weekly update a service to the client, or protection for you?
How much detail does a client really want about the cause?
In Brazil, do people expect an apology before the facts? Is it the same with an American client?
Have you ever received a status update that was actually good? What did the person do?
What is harder for you: the bad news, or saying it in English?
Sofia's client asked her to teach the format to other suppliers. Would that happen in your company?
Who taught you how to report progress at work — or did nobody?

wrapup.title: Before you go
items: Which three words from today will you use in a real call this week?
Say the four moves of a status update, in order.
Think of one job of yours right now. Which of the four moves is the one you usually skip?
